title: 10. NLP, Transformers & LLMs: Multi-Head Attention: Multiple Perspectives
summary: Goal: Understand why multiple attention heads are better than one.

sections.title: Why Multiple Heads?
sections.body:
**Goal**: Understand why multiple attention heads are better than one.

### Single Attention Head Limitation

```
Single Head:
  "The cat sat on the mat"
  
  One attention pattern:
  • Might focus on syntax (verb-noun relations)
  • OR semantic meaning
  • OR positional relationships
  
  But not ALL at once!
```

### Multi-Head Solution

```
8 Heads (BERT-base has 12!):
  Head 1: Focuses on syntactic structure
  Head 2: Captures semantic similarity
  Head 3: Learns positional patterns
  Head 4: Identifies named entities
  Head 5: Tracks coreferences
  ...
  
Each head learns different patterns!
```

sections.title: Core Idea
sections.body:
**Analogy**: Committee of Experts

```
Question: "What is this sentence about?"

Single Expert (1 head):
  • Gives one perspective
  • Might miss important aspects

Committee of Experts (multi-head):
  • Expert 1 (syntax): "Subject-verb agreement"
  • Expert 2 (semantics): "It's about animals"
  • Expert 3 (style): "Formal writing"
  • Expert 4 (context): "Part of a story"
  
  → Combine all perspectives → Better understanding!
```

sections.title: Mathematical Formulation
sections.body:
### Single-Head Attention (recap):
$$
\text{head} = \text{Attention}(QW^Q, KW^K, VW^V)
$$

### Multi-Head Attention:

**Step 1**: Create h separate attention heads
$$
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)
$$

Where $i = 1, 2, ..., h$ (number of heads)

**Step 2**: Concatenate all heads
$$
\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, ..., \text{head}_h)W^O
$$

**Complete Formula**:
$$
\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, ..., \text{head}_h)W^O
$$
$$
\text{where } \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)
$$

sections.title: Dimension Mathematics
sections.body:
### Example: BERT-base Configuration

```
d_model = 768    (model dimension)
h = 12           (number of heads)
d_k = d_v = 768 / 12 = 64  (per-head dimension)

Each head works in 64 dimensions
12 heads × 64 = 768 dimensions total

Why split?
• Keeps total parameter count manageable
• Each head specializes in lower-dimensional space
• Concatenation reconstructs full dimensionality
```

### Projection Matrices per Head:

```
For each head i:
  W_i^Q: (d_model × d_k) = (768 × 64)
  W_i^K: (d_model × d_k) = (768 × 64)
  W_i^V: (d_model × d_v) = (768 × 64)

Output projection:
  W^O: (h * d_v × d_model) = (768 × 768)

Total parameters per multi-head layer:
  3 * h * d_model * d_k + d_model²
  = 3 * 12 * 768 * 64 + 768²
  ≈ 2.36 million parameters
```

sections.title: Architecture Diagram
sections.body:
```
Input: X (batch, seq_len, d_model)
│
├─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Head 1                             │
│  Q₁ = X W₁^Q  K₁ = X W₁^K  V₁ = X W₁^V
│  Attention₁ = softmax(Q₁K₁ᵀ/√d_k)V₁│
│  Output₁: (batch, seq_len, d_k=64) │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Head 2                             │
│  Q₂ = X W₂^Q  K₂ = X W₂^K  V₂ = X W₂^V
│  Attention₂ = softmax(Q₂K₂ᵀ/√d_k)V₂│
│  Output₂: (batch, seq_len, d_k=64) │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ...                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Head 12                            │
│  Output₁₂: (batch, seq_len, d_k=64)│
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ↓
    Concatenate all heads
    (batch, seq_len, 768)
         │
         ↓
    Linear projection W^O
         │
         ↓
    Output: (batch, seq_len, d_model=768)
```

sections.title: PyTorch Implementation
sections.body:
```python
class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0, "d_model must be divisible by num_heads"
        
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_k = d_model // num_heads  # Dimension per head
        
        # Linear projections for all heads (combined)
        self.W_Q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_K = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_V = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        
        # Output projection
        self.W_O = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
    
    def split_heads(self, x):
        """
        Split into multiple heads.
        Input:  (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        Output: (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        """
        batch_size, seq_len, d_model = x.size()
        x = x.view(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_k)
        return x.transpose(1, 2)  # (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
    
    def combine_heads(self, x):
        """
        Combine multiple heads.
        Input:  (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        Output: (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        """
        batch_size, num_heads, seq_len, d_k = x.size()
        x = x.transpose(1, 2)  # (batch, seq_len, num_heads, d_k)
        return x.contiguous().view(batch_size, seq_len, self.d_model)
    
    def forward(self, query, key, value, mask=None):
        batch_size = query.size(0)
        
        # Linear projections
        Q = self.W_Q(query)  # (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        K = self.W_K(key)
        V = self.W_V(value)
        
        # Split into multiple heads
        Q = self.split_heads(Q)  # (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        K = self.split_heads(K)
        V = self.split_heads(V)
        
        # Scaled dot-product attention
        scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / np.sqrt(self.d_k)
        
        if mask is not None:
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)
        
        attention_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
        
        # Apply attention to values
        attention_output = torch.matmul(attention_weights, V)
        # Shape: (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        
        # Combine heads
        output = self.combine_heads(attention_output)
        # Shape: (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        
        # Final linear projection
        output = self.W_O(output)
        
        return output, attention_weights
```

sections.title: What Do Different Heads Learn?
sections.body:
### Empirical Observations from BERT:

**Head Types** (discovered through analysis):

```
Syntactic Heads:
• Head 3: Tracks subject-verb relationships
• Head 7: Identifies noun phrases
• Head 9: Detects prepositional phrases

Semantic Heads:
• Head 1: Captures word similarity
• Head 5: Identifies synonyms/antonyms
• Head 11: Understands context

Positional Heads:
• Head 2: Focuses on nearby words
• Head 4: Captures long-range dependencies
• Head 8: Attends to specific positions (e.g., [CLS], [SEP])

Coreference Heads:
• Head 6: Resolves pronoun references
• Head 10: Tracks entity mentions

Special Token Heads:
• Head 12: Attends to [CLS] for classification
```

### Example Visualization:

```
Sentence: "The cat sat on the mat because it was tired"

Head 1 (Syntax):
  The → cat (determiner-noun)
  cat → sat (subject-verb)
  
Head 2 (Semantics):
  cat → animal concepts
  mat → furniture concepts
  
Head 3 (Coreference):
  it → cat (pronoun resolution!)
  
Head 4 (Position):
  Each word → nearby words (window-based)
```

sections.title: Key Advantages
sections.body:
### 1. Representational Power
```
Multiple perspectives capture different linguistic phenomena:
• Syntax + Semantics + Position simultaneously
• Rich, multi-faceted representations
```

### 2. Redundancy & Robustness
```
If one head fails/doesn't learn well:
• Other heads can compensate
• More robust to noise
```

### 3. Specialization
```
Each head can specialize:
• Division of labor
• More efficient learning
```

### 4. Better Gradients
```
Multiple paths for backpropagation:
• Reduces vanishing gradient problem
• Faster, more stable training
```

sections.title: Parameter Count Comparison
sections.body:
```
Single-Head Attention:
  W^Q: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  W^K: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  W^V: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  Total: 3 × 768² = 1,769,472 parameters

Multi-Head Attention (12 heads):
  W^Q: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  W^K: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  W^V: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  W^O: d_model × d_model = 768 × 768
  Total: 4 × 768² = 2,359,296 parameters

Only 33% more parameters for 12× the modeling capacity!
```

sections.title: Hyperparameters
sections.body:
### Number of Heads (h)

```
Small models:
  • GPT-2 small: 12 heads
  • BERT-base: 12 heads
  
Large models:
  • GPT-2 large: 16 heads
  • BERT-large: 16 heads
  • GPT-3: 96 heads (!)
  
Rule of thumb:
  • h should divide d_model evenly
  • Common: 8, 12, 16 heads
  • Larger model → more heads
```

### Head Dimension (d_k)

```
Typical values:
  • d_k = 64 (most common)
  • d_k = 128 (larger models)
  
Constraint: d_k = d_model / h
  
Example:
  • BERT-base: 768 / 12 = 64
  • BERT-large: 1024 / 16 = 64
  • GPT-3: 12288 / 96 = 128
```

sections.title: Computational Complexity
sections.body:
### Time Complexity:

```
Single sequence of length n:
  • Attention matrix: O(n²d_k) per head
  • Multi-head (h heads): O(h × n²d_k)
  • Since h × d_k = d_model: O(n²d_model)

Practical impact:
  • Sequence length dominates!
  • n=512: 262,144 comparisons
  • n=2048: 4,194,304 comparisons
  • Quadratic scaling is the bottleneck
```

### Memory Complexity:

```
Attention matrix per head: O(n²)
Multi-head: O(h × n²)

For BERT-base (12 heads):
  • n=512: ~3MB per attention matrix
  • Total: ~36MB just for attention weights
  
This is why long sequences are expensive!
```

sections.title: Common Patterns
sections.body:
### Cross-Attention vs Self-Attention

**Self-Attention** (BERT, GPT):
```python
# Query, Key, Value all from same sequence
output = attention(query=X, key=X, value=X)
```

**Cross-Attention** (Encoder-Decoder):
```python
# Query from decoder, Key/Value from encoder
output = attention(
    query=decoder_state,
    key=encoder_output,
    value=encoder_output
)
```

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
### Key Points:
```
✓ Multiple heads = multiple perspectives
✓ Each head works in lower dimension (d_k)
✓ Concatenation reconstructs full dimension
✓ Heads specialize in different patterns
✓ Only ~33% more parameters than single head
✓ Critical for SOTA performance
```

### Configuration Guidelines:
```
• Heads: 8-16 for most models
• d_k: 64 typical
• Always: d_model = num_heads × d_k
• More heads → more capacity but more compute
```
